title: Management and challenges in access and diagnosis of drinking water services in Rural Areas of Latin América
authors: Acosta-González A.; Jimenez-Junca C.A.; Gallardo-Salas M.A.
abstract: Ensuring access to potable water, basic sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) in Latin America, particularly in rural areas, remains challenging. In 2022, 8.4% of the population lacked safe drinking water, while 74.6% had basic sanitation. Regulatory approaches vary but are generally nascent, facing significant water quality challenges from agricultural runoff, industrial discharges, and mining activities. Inadequate wastewater treatment leads to bacteriological pollution. Over- extraction of groundwater, unplanned urban growth, and limited resources exacerbate pollution and water stress. Monitoring and enforcement are hindered by outdated infrastructure and inadequate training. Critical water quality parameters are inconsistently measured, and delayed sample processing compromises microbiological analyses. Education and training in water management, infrastructure improvements, and investment are imperative to address climate change impacts and social inequalities. Additionally, unplanned urban expansion puts further pressure on water resources in peri- urban areas. © 2026, IGI Global Scientific Publishing. All rights reserved.

title: Government policies toward providing safe drinking water to the public
authors: Yadav P.; Yadav K.; Saxena M.; Singh I.
abstract: The national drinking water programs should address the monitoring issues that can affect data sampling, self-reporting, data quality and accuracy, as well as adequate frequency for evaluating the water sustainability systems. India is distinguished by its extensive rural water database, the Integrated Management Information System (IMIS), which conducts annual monitoring of drinking water coverage, water quality, and related program components from the habitation level to the state, district, and national levels. In recent years, there has been a notable increase in debate regarding policy improvements and their implementation. Various narratives related to water policy and discourses have attracted significant scholarly attention. These narratives cover a range of topics, including groundwater management challenges, access to clean water as well as sanitation, gender equity in the assessment of water and sanitation, integrated water resource management, and interstate river management. Additionally, global concerns about water security and climate change are adding a fresh perspective to the discussion. Natural disasters have had a significant negative impact on freshwater supplies, potentially causing water shortages in many parts of the world. In response, current water management reforms have placed a strong emphasis on effective policymaking to improve overall water governance, management, and planning. This chapter focuses on the structure of India's national water policies in terms of their individual components. © 2025 Veer Singh and Ashish Kumar. All rights reserved.

title: Legal Empowerment in Informal Settlements: Grassroots Experiences in the Global South
authors: Di Giovanni A.; Bercovich L.
abstract: This book investigates grassroots, community-led justice strategies — known as legal empowerment — being used to promote the human rights of people living in informal settlements in the Global South. Residents of informal settlements, also known as slums or favelas, encounter a complex array of human rights violations; from systemic discrimination by public officials, to threats to physical security from forced evictions, or arbitrary arrests, to a lack of access to basic services such as housing, water, sanitation and education. This book shows how grassroots justice organizations around the world are working with residents to defend their rights and secure more dignified living conditions. Drawing on original empirical research across 10 countries in Africa, Asia and Latin America, the book demonstrates how legal empowerment can put residents at the centre of holistic approaches to urban development and confront exclusionary and undemocratic systems of governance. The book encompasses practical recommendations and strategies such as rights-based approaches to informality, participation, community mobilization and litigation. Bridging the gaps between the law on the books and the harsh realities of informality on the ground, this book will be an important read for researchers, practitioners and policymakers, working in realms of social and economic rights, access to justice and urban poverty and development. © 2025 International Development Research Centre and Namati.

title: Blockchain and Water Supply Chain: Opportunities, Challenges and Innovations
authors: Batta P.; Wasson V.; Sardar S.
abstract: This chapter investigates how blockchain technology delivers better efficiency and protection measures with increased sustainability for water supply chain operations, addressing major difficulties to create adaptable water distribution frameworks. Multiple systems, along with devices from IoT sensors and legacy software platforms, characterize the operation of the water supply chain. Existing literature highlights the role of blockchain in enhancing transparency, security and efficiency in the water supply chain through IoT integration, smart contracts and hybrid networks. Using a hybrid blockchain method enabled stakeholders to achieve public transparency and private data protection, which enhanced interoperability between them. Smart contracts perform automatic water regulation compliance that maintains quality control standards. Regulatory authorities maintain unmodifiable access to records, which helps them enforce compliance and policy regulations. Water quality and distribution monitoring becomes accurate with the deployment of IoT sensors, which also streamlines financial operations by automating billing, leakage detection and policy implementation. © ISTE Ltd 2025. All rights reserved.

title: An Investigation into India’s Experience in Reducing Child Mortality: A Gender Perspective
authors: Ram U.; Kumar P.; Ananya K.V.
abstract: India surpassed China and became the most populated country recently. The population of India is expected to further grow for several decades before it stabilizes. The recent past has shown remarkable improvements in socio-economic development indicators for India, yet, they are far from satisfactory levels. India’s health care service provisions, particularly in the public sector, continues to face challenges in terms of both access and quality. India is one of the few countries where gender plays a vital role for one’s socio-economic and health outcomes. Thus, India’s overall achievement in improving the health of its people is certainly laudable; however, it becomes essential to learn whether these benefits are shared equally across population subgroups. Between 1950 and 2020, India’s population grew from 357 million to 1396 million; a nearly 300% rise in 7-decades, with an increase from a total of 15.7 million to 23.1 million annual live births during the same time. The childhood mortality has reduced substantially: infant mortality rate reduced substantially from 181.2 in 1950 to 26.6 per 1000 live births in 2020, and the under-5 mortality rate, reduced from around 300 in 1950 to 32.6 per 1000 live births in 2020. In 1950, a newborn in India, on an average, lived 41.7 years which rose to 70.2 years in 2020. Along with this progress in mortality reductions, household’s living conditions and other socio-economic development indicators have also shown laudable improvements; 95% of the households in 2019–21 have access to improved source of drinking water and 69% had access to basic sanitation services. Women’s literacy rate increased from only 2 in every 5 women aged 15–49 literate in 1992–93 to 4 in every 5 women in 2019–21 and total fertility rate declined from 3.4 children per women to 2.0 during the same period. Over 85% of the mothers received antenatal care from a skilled provider(s) in 2019–21, substantial increase from 50% in 1992–93. The institutional delivery increased from about one-quarter in 1992–93 to 89% in 2019–21. Early initiation of breastfeeding has risen more than four-folds and exclusive breastfeeding has risen by one and a half times and at the same time, the coverage of full immunization has increased to more than three-quarters in 2019–21. There has been consistent improvement in the mortality indicator as well as socio-economic and health care utilization, however, gender differential is persistent, mostly to the disadvantage of female children, and this is regardless of time period. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2025.

title: Status and Issues Related to the Implementation of Integrated River Basin Management in Malaysia
authors: Lim C.H.; Teo F.Y.
abstract: The findings of a desktop study carried out concerning the status and issues on the implementation of Integrated River Basin Management (IRBM) in Malaysia can be categorised under thirteen (13) main aspects; namely, policy, legislation, institution, financing, water assessment and allocation, pollution control, flood management, drought management, river basin and land use planning, river basin information system, R&D on IRBM, river basin monitoring, and stakeholder participation. Enabling Mechanisms In 2012, a National Water Resources Policy (NWRP) was formulated to guide water resources management in the country, whereby the approach in integrated river basin management will be through the adoption of IWRM principles at the river basin level. This NWRP is currently under review and has been renamed as National Water Policy (NWP). The key policy issues encountered in Malaysia are as follows: i) slow implementation of all the action plans as stated in NWP at state-level, especially for states that do not have any specific state-level water resource management policy, and ii) challenges in forging Federal/State level partnerships to implement NWP effectively due to political differences. In terms of legislation, the various matters related to water are covered under many separate and uncoordinated legislation where most of these laws are either outdated or with gaps and in some instances overlapping each other. In 2010, a draft National Water Resources Law (NWRL) was developed as a ‘model law’ to ensure uniformity for all states in Peninsular Malaysia and to supersede the current Waters Act 1920. The Federal Constitution has clearly defined the jurisdiction and alignment of the Federal and State Governments over water as a resource. States have jurisdiction over water resources and related aspects such as land, forests, agriculture, rivers, and water bodies. However, the Federal Government has jurisdiction over the following matters related to water resources-i) international treaties and agreements; ii) transboundary rivers; iii) transfer of water (if not resolved between states); iv) data, information collection and management; v) scientific research; and vi) setting of national standards, safety, and security. As for the financing mechanism, after the enactment of the Water Services Industry Act (WSIA) in 2006, the Federal Government is now responsible for managing and financing the water services sector while the state is left with the responsibility to finance and manage the water resource sector. Water Resources and Water Hazards Water assessment needs to be carried out to ascertain the available water resources in a River basins are the natural accounting units for water management. However, political, and administrative decisions relating to water management are usually made according to jurisdictional boundaries that do not coincide with that of river basins. A river basin plan is a strategic action plan for the integrated management of the water and related land resources in the basin. The plan will normally be relevant for several years and will facilitate the co-ordination of specific works by the relevant agencies who shall incorporate the required works into their annual work plans accompanied by specified actions and detailed budgets. The key river basin and land use planning issues that have been identified are as follows: i) inadequate legislative support for IRBM-compliant land use control in the river basin, ii) land use control at the local authority level is not guided by a river basin plan, iii) inadequate technical capacity to monitor the implementation of river basin master plan and iv) loss of river biodiversity. IWRM, in the context of a river basin, is about the management of available water resources in a river basin for an optimum outcome among different competing water users. Thus, comprehensive, accurate, and timely information is necessary for objective planning, decision-making, and gaining support from competing river basin stakeholders. Deciding on what to report, to whom, and how to communicate the report to the relevant stakeholders is the most important step. However, there are still issues related to the river basin information system, such as those identified below: i) too much information but lack of useful information, ii) inappropriate selection and choice of information management tools, iii) lack of coordination in information dissemination for national-level decision making, and iv) limited access to the public despite of much promises and publicity by the various agencies. There are many issues related to IRBM that need additional research, especially in relation to the local context. This is because the R&D results and experiences from other countries cannot be applied directly to Malaysia since the local institutional and legal framework is different from those in other countries. For effective water resource management, it is essential that monitoring be carried out to assess the availability of water resources, water quality, water use, and pollution discharges in a river basin. Information management of the monitored data is additionally necessary to ensure that water resource assessment, ii) fragmented and non-uniform state legislation governing water allocation, and iii) water allocation in many states is not guided by an IRBM Plan and IWRM principles. Managing water pollution is one of the most critical challenges to the sustainable management of water resources. Pollution is increasing rapidly due to urbanisation, industrialisation, and population growth. The appraisal of the water quality in each river basin is based on the Water Quality Index (WQI) consisting of parameters such as dissolved oxygen (DO), biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), chemical oxygen demand (COD), ammoniacal nitrogen (NH3-N), suspended solids (SS) and pH. There are 189 river systems in Malaysia of which 85 are prone to frequent flooding. Flooding has become a national issue in Malaysia as the nation’s economy and population have grown over the years and developments started to encroach into river corridors and flood plains which has resulted in increased incidences of floods. The key flood management issues are as follows: i) increased incidences and costs of flood damages due to increased development in urban areas and encroachment of development into urban river corridors, ii) uncontrolled development in flood-prone areas, and iii) impact of climate change which resulted in increased rainfall intensity. Unlike the situation in arid countries, drought is not a major issue in a tropical country like Malaysia with its abundant rainfall. However, due to the natural, annual variability of rainfall, there may be some periods in some years where a prolonged period of low rainfall may affect the amount of water stored in the dams to provide for potable and irrigation water supply in specific areas or regions. River Basin Management basin approach that can be disseminated to all the river basin stakeholders and be easily available at the all relevant agencies’ websites. Stakeholder participation is important because stakeholders who are interested in, and accepting of the water resource management system, can ensure its sustainable implementation on the ground. Communication with all relevant stakeholders is also important to raise the awareness of the river basin stakeholders and educate them on the benefits of their participation in the management of the river basin. © 2025 IAHR.

title: Carbon territoriality at the land-water interface
authors: Miller M.A.
abstract: Large volumes of organic carbon are stored in wetland ecosystems such as mangrove forests, peatlands, salt marshes and seagrass meadows. Efforts to mitigate anthropogenic climate change are transforming the governance of these naturally saturated carbon sinks. Scientific and market valuations of wetlands as carbon have prompted diverse experimentation with carbon sequestration projects and offset programs. These activities may displace wetland-reliant communities and add to societal equalities. This perspective paper develops the concept of carbon territoriality to explore emerging spaces of climate governance in wetlands. It moves beyond terra-centric policy debates tied to fixed and flat landscapes by integrating literature on the dynamic (sub)surface and atmospheric territorial dimensions of carbon. It posits that combining scientific knowledge of fixed carbon stocks with the inherited knowledge of coastal and riparian communities about fluid land–water connections could foster more inclusive and equitable forms of climate stewardship within biogeophysically relevant boundaries. © 2024 The Author

title: Primary Care Dentistry in Hong Kong
authors: Fung M.H.T.
abstract: Primary care dental services in Hong Kong are provided by the dental team that consists of dentists, dental therapists, dental hygienists, dental surgery assistants and dental technicians. Despite a majority of dental services being provided by practitioners working in the private sector and non-governmental organisations (NGOs), the government has played a leading role in the development of primary care services and places emphasis on oral health promotion and prioritises resources to provide emergency dental services and special care dentistry services. Starting from 1961, water fluoridation has been available in the water supply. This has been recognized by the WHO and FDI World Dental Federation as a safe and effective measure for the prevention of dental caries. There has been a continuous development of dental services by the Department of Health to meet the needs of the public. The School Dental Care Service provides comprehensive care for the primary school children. Emergency dental services for pain relief are available to the general public at government dental clinics. The Oral Health Promotion Division provides oral health education to the public. The Community Special Dental Service oversees the provision of special care dentistry services for people who have difficulty to access for general dental services. Eligible institutionalised elderly and adults with intellectual disabilities or autism can receive subsidized services provided by the designated NGOs. For people with financial hardships, subsidised dental services can be provided by the Department of Social Welfare under the Dental Grant of the Comprehensive Social Security Assistance Scheme. Through the Elderly Health Care Voucher Scheme and Community Care Fund Elderly Dental Assistance Programme, eligible older adults can receive subsidised primary care services at private clinics. Primary Care Directory has been established to facilitate the residents to seek various primary healthcare services that are available in the private setting. The Primary Healthcare Blueprints have highlighted a series of reform initiatives to formulate the direction and strategies of primary healthcare development in Hong Kong. The Working Group on Oral Health and Dental Care was established to review the current dental service provision and all the existing government-funded programmes regarding their objectives, scopes of service and service delivery models. An Interim Report has been published that includes the strategic directions recommended by the Working Group. With the collaborations between the Government and the practitioners working in both public and private sectors, primary care dentistry services have been evolving to target the improvement of oral health of the general public. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2025.

title: Smart Village Panchayat-An e-Governance system
authors: Harshavarthan E.; Ayyanathan N.
abstract: This is a smart village panchayat automated complaint management system, an effort to substitute the traditional manual complaint handling in the governance of local complaints. It allows citizens to post complaints about those basic services that are crucial for public service, such as street lighting, water supply, garbage disposal, and road maintenance. Through integrating location-based services such as Google Maps, the system enhances the precision and efficiency in complaint resolution regarding pinpointing the exact location of issues. This application provides updates, so that citizens are able to track the process of their complaint from its submission and its resolution. The inclusion of mechanisms of feedback ensures that authorities stay accountable, and this leads to a loop of continuous improvement. The digitization process seeks to reduce inefficiency, eradicate corruption, and make local governance more transparent because earlier procedures-lagging and error-prone-may be eradicated. The project represents massive strides in local governance modernization for the country, thus enhancing responsiveness and effectiveness in the operations of Panchayats. The smart village Panchayat initiative is a digital transformation project for rural Panchayat functioning, creating new pathways in the innovation of local village organizations in India. Panchayats, being the backbones of local self-governments, are engaged in a large number of public services like water supply, sanitation, and infrastructure development. However, with the traditional Panchayat systems comes inefficiency due to the principle of manual processes and the lack of transparency concerning matters dealt with, citizen participation, and everyday functioning. © 2025 IEEE.

title: Blockchain-powered DeFi: Transforming Water Project Financing for a Sustainable Future
authors: Shyamala R.; Prabakaran D.; Dhaya C.; Chaarumathi S.; Perumal U.; Kumaran V.S.
abstract: This chapter describes how decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols, liquidity pools and decentralized autonomous organizations can revolutionize water project finance by capital universalization, middleman elimination, and traceable and instant transactions. Green finance emphasizes investment that directs long-term environmental, social and governance (ESG) objectives. Water infrastructure is one of the primary drivers of green growth, and blockchain-based DeFi applications improve ESG. Traditional models of water infrastructure investment finance have been marred by numerous obstacles that limit their efficiency, coverage and scalability. There are several DeFi models in existence today,each trying to solve various needs of finance, from lending and borrowing to decentralized exchange, stablecoins and yield farming. Water infrastructure schemes such as building sustainable water supply systems, desalination plants, irrigation systems and wastewater treatment plants are costly and require massive capital investment. DeFi allows water infrastructure projects to be tokenized and investors to invest in fractionality. © ISTE Ltd 2025. All rights reserved.

title: The Effects of Politics on Service Delivery
authors: Mabizela H.
abstract: Politics and service delivery are fundamental factors that influence the quality and efficiency of governance in every country, including South Africa. The interplay between the two conceptions affects the efficacy of government policy in meeting citizens’ needs. Service delivery often encompasses the provision of essential services such as water, housing, sanitation, healthcare, education, and infrastructure that deeply shape the lives of the citizens and determines the legitimacy of government. However, politics influences service delivery, both negatively and positively. While political leadership impacts governmental decision-making and resource allocation to address the demands and expectations of citizens, political dynamics introduces challenges that undermine the ability of government to delivery services effectively. This chapter examines the present state of service delivery and the role of politics in advancing the development post-apartheid in the context of the South African government. The chapter also acknowledges that political leadership can facilitate service delivery by establishing clear priorities that promote the necessary reforms and guarantee that the public service meets the requirements of the population. © 2026 Hlengiwe Mabizela and Nirmala Dorasamy.

title: The Road to Resilience: Integrating Maintenance Strategies into Asset Management for Water and Wastewater Utilities
authors: Motala I.; Singh A.
abstract: Water and wastewater utilities face growing challenges in maintaining aging infrastructure while meeting service targets and controlling costs. To address this, the Region of Peel developed a structured, standards-based approach to maintenance management, emphasizing governance, business processes, data, and technology integration. Through a tailored maturity assessment aligned with ISO 55000 and the GFMAM framework, the Region identified key gaps and created a roadmap for improvement. Findings highlight measurable improvements in operational efficiency, including reduced unplanned work, increased asset reliability, and enhanced planning and scheduling capabilities. By adopting best practices such as reliability-centered maintenance (RCM) and leveraging analytics, Peel demonstrated how maintenance can evolve into a strategic enabler of operational excellence. This work offers actionable insights for utilities seeking to strengthen their maintenance programs, align with industry standards, and achieve sustainable service delivery. Copyright ©2025 Water Environment Federation.

title: Unveiling Market Manipulation in Eu Energy Markets - Insights from Acer Enforcement Cases
authors: Lakic E.; Jeriha J.; Medved T.; Vucic D.; Topic D.; Knezevic G.
abstract: Market manipulation poses significant challenges to the integrity and transparency of EU wholesale energy markets. This paper examines REMIT enforcement decisions published by the European Union Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators (ACER), identifying key trends, manipulation tactics, and regulatory responses. By analysing publicly available ACER enforcement cases, this study provides insights into the most common market abuse practices, including capacity withholding, wash trades, and cross-border manipulation, as well as disparities in enforcement activity across Member States. The findings highlight the growing role of fines in deterring market abuse, with 2024 recording a € 73 million penalty-the highest to date. With the introduction of REMIT II, regulatory enforcement is expected to intensify, introducing stricter reporting obligations, broader market coverage, and enhanced investigative powers for ACER. This paper contributes to energy market regulation literature by providing a comprehensive review of REMIT enforcement cases and recommending measures to strengthen market integrity. The findings serve as a resource for policymakers, regulators, and market participants seeking to enhance transparency, detect manipulation more effectively, and ensure a competitive energy market.  © 2025 IEEE.

title: Process Safety Consequences of Biogas Release and Fire Scenarios at Wastewater Treatment Facilities: Ensuring Safe Distances for Occupied Buildings using Advanced Python Modelling
authors: Masango P.; Griffin L.
abstract: This work on chemical explosions is premised on Biogas (facilities), especially its production and storage in the wastewater industry. The process safety considerations in storage tanks and other gas holders, also applies to entire chemical storage facilities across the chemical process industry where DSEAR and/or COMAH regulations may apply. Loss of control which could mean loss of containment of flammable or highly reactive chemicals such as biogas pose significant (explosion and fire) risks to process safety, environmental health, and asset safety. This python model will be useful for simpler first stage consequence modelling and will complement the platforms already in use, out there. The importance of accurate, economically affordable explosion modelling cannot be overstated. Accessibility can lead to broader availability o safety protocols, resulting in general improvement in the provision of safety simulations. Previous research and commercial software have provided valuable insights, yet there remains some work that advances this area of process engineering as well as improve competences internal to any organisation that is interested in software development in this area. In future greater advances and better economics will be had due to better access to similar software. Our study aims to offer locally accessible and more economic application as well as improve the accuracies by introducing a new perspective on explosion modelling. By leveraging advanced computational techniques and comprehensive data analysis, we propose a model that offers improved reliability and safety. This work builds upon the foundation laid by previous researchers, acknowledging their contributions while striving for greater precision. © 2025 IChemE.

title: Water pollution: sources, causes, and effects
authors: Tamrakar R.K.; Butoliya S.; Upadhyay K.
abstract: Water is an indispensable resource vital for the survival of all forms of life, economic development, and overall well-being. However, with escalating anthropogenic activities, water pollution has emerged as one of the most pressing global environmental challenges. This document delves into comprehensive methodologies for assessing and ensuring water quality while presenting actionable solutions for mitigating pollution. The analysis begins by categorizing water quality measurement techniques into physical, chemical, and biological parameters. Detailed methodologies, including advanced technologies such as IoT-enabled real-time monitoring and molecular metagenomics, are discussed to provide a robust framework for water quality assessment. Sampling strategies, including grab, composite, and passive sampling, further underscore the precision required in environmental monitoring. The document also explores preventive and remedial approaches for water pollution. These include municipal wastewater treatment, industrial effluent management, precision agricultural practices, and erosion control. Emphasis is placed on leveraging green infrastructure, technological innovations, and international cooperation to address water contamination comprehensively. The synthesis highlights the necessity of public awareness and legislative enforcement to align individual, community, and industrial practices with sustainable water resource management. By adopting these measures, it is possible to mitigate the adverse impacts of pollution, protect aquatic ecosystems, and secure clean water for future generations. This study serves as a call to action for multidisciplinary collaboration and the integration of science, policy, and education to address the water crisis effectively. In recent years, the quality of the world’s water supply has received more attention. Due to its irreplaceable nature, water is stored in a separate system. Both the biological cycle and the economic cycle rely on the water cycle for their fundamental dynamics. The proportion of freshwater to total water in the water cycle is only 2.5%. All living things require water, so it is clear that this commodity is extremely important. Without water, there is no possibility of survival. Freshwater ecosystems, food security, sustainable development, and, by extension, the survival of humankind, all depend on an abundant supply of high-quality water. Pressure on already scarce pure water supplies is increased when that water is polluted. To purify 1 L of wastewater requires the use of eight gallons of potable water. Humans have an inherent requirement for access to clean water. According to the World Health Organization, about 80% of all infectious illnesses (bacteria, viruses, and parasites) are spread through contact with water. Waste and pollution of this essential natural resource are major contributors to global warming, and humans are largely to blame. It is imperative that people everywhere receive water pollution education and consciousness training in order to help mitigate this crisis. The emphasis of this study is on the origins of various water pollutants and their current distribution throughout ecosystems and the natural environment. This investigation is expected to add to the existing body of writing on the topic and help lessen the burden of pollution on our planet’s water supplies. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

title: We have the evidence but governments must now build the systems to deliver on hand hygiene
authors: Esteves Mills J.; Gordon B.; Denny L.; Thomas A.; Cole A.O.; Lee-Llacer A.; Hickling S.; Ababu A.K.; Kwakye A.; Mohamed A.; Palomares A.; Paynter N.; Prasad-Gautam O.; Shrestha S.; Kalubula P.; Caruso B.A.; Freeman M.C.; Wolfe M.K.; Panthi S.R.; Balane M.A.L.; Villasenor J.M.; Bartolomeus K.; Eshofonie A.; Magtibay B.; Bouare S.; Doumbia D.; Nkosha K.; Ojha R.; Abaidoo S.; Kutane W.; Toure M.; Sangare I.; Limbu S.; Kabir A.; Ranjouria S.; Mulemba D.; Alzubaidy S.; Kokshagina O.; Heiss L.; Minelli E.; Nachinab C.; Cumming O.

title: Service Delivery and the Pulse of Citizen Satisfaction in Urban Governance of Bangladesh
authors: Mollah M.A.H.
abstract: This book offers a comparative analysis of municipal service delivery in four major Bangladeshi cities: Dhaka, Chittagong, Khulna, and Rajshahi. Using the SERVQUAL model, it evaluates service quality through five dimensions—Tangibles, Reliability, Responsiveness, Assurance, and Empathy—providing a detailed understanding of citizen satisfaction in varied urban settings. The book’s strength lies in its comparative framework, which examines the distinct challenges and governance structures of each city. This analysis identifies common issues while uncovering unique dynamics, enabling a thorough exploration of service delivery systems. It highlights effective practices and areas for improvement, fostering a balanced view of urban governance. Key municipal services such as street lighting, waste management, water supply, sewerage systems, and birth registration are assessed in detail. By focusing on practical reforms and innovations, the book bridges academic research with real-world application, offering actionable insights for policymakers, urban planners, and practitioners. With its emphasis on practical solutions and comparative insights, this book is an essential resource for those involved in urban development. It provides valuable lessons for enhancing service quality and citizen satisfaction, contributing to more effective governance in developing countries. © 2025 The Editor(s) (if applicable) and The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd.

title: Changes in Quality of Living Environment Due to Landuse Transformation in Rural Areas of Ahmedabad City, India
authors: Kothary S.
abstract: The idea of a living environment may sound abstract, but it becomes visible in the way people live day to day the quality of their housing, the work they do, their openness to modern practices, and the steady efforts they make to improve their standard of living. In this study, these aspects were examined through field research carried out in 23 villages situated in the peri-urban belt of Ahmedabad, India. Variables included dwelling type and density, fuels for domestic use, electricity, access to water, sanitation, transport, and household hygiene. To interpret the findings, the Drivera Pressurea Statea Impacta Response (DPSIR) framework was applied, which has been increasingly used in environmental and urban studies since 2020 (Benevolo & Romano, 2021; Rosado, 2024). The results show that urban growth and in-migration are major drivers, creating pressures on land, services, and infrastructure, which alter the state of settlements into congested, poorly serviced neighbourhoods. This produces impacts including waste build- up, ecological stress, and declining health, while responses from governance remain partial. These findings resonate with emerging work on peri-urban transformation and sustainable infrastructure in India (Kundu, 2021; UN-Habitat, 2022; World Bank, 2023; Singh & Sharma, 2024). © The Authors, published by EDP Sciences, 2025.

title: Environmental Determinants of Early Childhood Caries: A Narrative Synthesis of Observational Evidence and Implications for Global Policy
authors: Foláyan M.O.; Schroth R.J.; Olatosi O.; El Tantawi M.
abstract: Early childhood caries (ECC) remains a significant global health challenge, disproportionately affecting marginalized populations. While traditional research emphasizes behavioral and biological risk factors, emerging evidence highlights the critical role of environmental determinants. This narrative synthesis aims to highlight the role of environmental determinants as a risk factor for ECC pathogenesis. Environmental toxins (e.g., lead, perfluoroalkyl acids, tobacco smoke, air pollution) disrupt enamel development, impair salivary function, and compromise immune responses, directly increasing caries susceptibility. Environmental degradation, including air pollution, reduces ultraviolet B radiation exposure, limiting endogenous vitamin D synthesis that is vital for enamel mineralization and immune regulation. These risks are compounded in low- and middle-income countries, where structural inequities, inadequate sanitation, and climate disruptions exacerbate ECC burdens. We introduce ecovitality—the resilience of ecosystems supporting human health—as a novel framework linking ecological vitality to oral health. Degraded environments limit access to fluoridated water and nutrient-dense foods while promoting sugary diets and endocrine disruptors. A One Health approach is advocated to address interconnected environmental, social, and biological determinants of the risk for ECC. Despite global reductions in tobacco use and lead exposure, the Global Burden of Disease 2021 analysis reports stagnation in ECC prevalence. This underscores the critical need for longitudinal and mechanistic studies to establish causality, quantify the contributions of environmental controls, and explore how mitigating these risks can reduce the global ECC burden. Such evidence may promote interdisciplinary action to align oral health promotion for children with the Sustainable Development Goals. © 2025 by the authors.

title: INTEGRATED WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT IN ACHIEVING SDG 6: A COMPARATIVE STUDY
authors: Iraguha L.; Ofuyatan O.; Olukanni D.O.
abstract: Achieving global access to clean water is a worldwide challenge; most regions in developing countries have not met the sustainable development goal 6. This paper reviews how integrated water resources management strategies in Rwanda and Nigeria help to reach the target of SDG 6: Clean Water and Sanitation. This review systematically assessed recently published research papers, government reports, case studies across countries, and UN SDGs progress reports. Results show that while Nigeria currently faces more problems in policy execution, stakeholder involvement, and governance than Rwanda, there is significant potential for improvement. At the end of this comparative study, suggestions were made for success: stakeholders' holistic involvement, including the people themselves, sectors' cooperation, consistent funding to water resources management agencies and projects, and reduced institutional overlapping in responsibilities. These recommendations emphasize a robust governance framework and community-centered solutions for water-related challenges. Learning from both countries, this study gives insight that can be used with other countries to speed up the progress toward universal access to clean water and sanitation and broader sustainable development goals. © 2025 ISEC Press.

title: Farmers’ Climate Change Adaptation Strategies and the Role of Environmental Awareness and Education: A Review in Africa
authors: Ahmed M.N.Q.; Givens J.E.
abstract: Climate change is a global challenge. Even though climate change affects all countries, less-developed countries and poor peasant farmers are especially at risk and have difficulty adapting. Less-developed nations are home to an estimated 500 million small-scale farms, who provide sustenance for approximately two billion people. In addition, it is estimated that these small farms produce nearly 80 per cent of the food consumed in Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. Existing literature finds Africa is particularly susceptible to the effects of climate fluctuation and change, including rising sea levels, melting glaciers, threatened water supplies, leading to decreased agricultural output, increasing food insecurity, diminished biodiversity, intensifying erosion, drought, and flood. In Africa, smallholder farmers depend on agriculture, which relies on timely rainfall, and thus they increasingly experience the consequences of climate change. This chapter reviews the literature on smallholder farmers in Africa and climate change, focusing on their perceptions of climate change and their adaptation techniques. We also explore how various factors affect smallholder farmers’ perceptions of climate change and their adaptation strategies. Finally, we discuss the need to improve awareness and adaptation capacity. Although farmers in various African countries perceive climate change differently, the literature review reveals that they have some views in common. Most farmers observe changes in temperature and rainfall patterns in their area. They also report experiencing increasing floods and droughts and decreasing crop production. Diversification of crops, changing crops, planting drought-resistant crops, incorporating livestock into crop production, shifting the time of agricultural operations, homestead gardening, increasing irrigation, engaging in mixed farming, and migration are common adaptation strategies reported in African countries. We found various household-related factors (gender, age, education, marital status, family size, etc.), farm-related factors (farming experience, size of the farm, etc.), institutional factors (access to information, extension contact, etc.), as well as other factors (participation in a social group, training, etc.) are affecting local level adaptation strategies among farmers. We contend that farmers are the “front-liners” in adapting to climate change, and government agencies and other national and international organizations should continue their efforts to support them. Moreover, to contribute to the progress of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, farmers’ insights and experiences should be integrated in the dominant policies and plans, including coordination of education about climate change and adaptation strategies. Furthermore, we also advocate for emphasizing improving environmental awareness through environmental education particularly in this region to achieve effective adaptation. © 2025 The Editor(s) (if applicable) and The Author(s).

title: Assessing water consumption in Indian thermal power plants and parametric strategy for optimal usage: An explanatory approach using machine learning algorithms
authors: Das S.S.; Majumdar R.; Krishnan A.V.; Srikanth R.
abstract: The reliability of water supply resources is of utmost importance for the electricity sector, particularly for the cooling requirements in Steam Rankine Cycle (SRC)-based thermo-electric power plants. The study investigates the influence of specific power plant parameters, such as Cycles of Concentration (CoC) and Plant Load Factor (PLF), and meteorological conditions (such as temperature, humidity, and wind speed) on the specific water consumption (SWC) of Indian thermal power stations using Machine Learning (ML) based Decision Tree Algorithms. While regulations exist to reduce water consumption, the study highlights the underexplored potential of improving these power plant parameters, which are crucial for water use curtailment. By leveraging data-driven decision-making, the study identifies the order of importance for the significant variables that influence SWC in thermal power plants and highlights the necessity of optimizing these variables. The study concludes that an optimal operational range can be established by effectively controlling CoC and PLF, considering the local meteorological parameters, that yields minimal water consumption for power plant operations. The results derived from the Machine Learning algorithms possess intuitive validity, as confirmed by descriptive analysis and insights from domain experts, as well as previously published scholarly articles. This study is a testament to the practical effectiveness of machine learning tools in addressing socially important sustainability issues. © 2025 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.

title: Assessment of the quality and availability of groundwater for domestic purposes in Likupang National Tourism Strategic Area (KSPN), Indonesia
authors: Tansil A.P.; Wilopo W.; Abdurrachman F.
abstract: East Likupang, as one of the regions developing the national tourism area in Indonesia, must fulfill adequate tourism aspects, especially in terms of clean water needs, both for tourism needs and for domestic purposes (hygiene and sanitation) for residents in the tourism area. The research collected 20 samples at two spring points and 18 groundwater wells spread throughout East Likupang District. Measurements of groundwater depth and analysis using ArcGIS were carried out to see the direction of groundwater flow, which was then linked to regional hydrogeological conditions to assess the availability of groundwater at the research location. In addition, groundwater samples were assessed by the Indonesia Minister of Health Regulation No. 2 of 2023 on Implementing Regulations of Government Regulation No. 66 of 2014 on Environmental Health and analyzed with the main physicochemical parameters, such as e-Coli, total coliform, TDS, turbidity, pH, nitrite (NO2-), chromium (Cr6+), iron (Fe) and manganese (Mn). Laboratory test results show that most water samples at all spring and groundwater well sampling locations are not suitable for use as a source of clean water. This can be seen from the results of microbiological parameter tests, which do not meet existing standards. However, if we only refer to physical and chemical parameters, most of these groundwater sources are still suitable for use as water sources for domestic needs. These results indicate that villages, the main locations for tourism development, still have water access and water quality sufficient to support domestic water needs and tourism purposes.  © Published under licence by IOP Publishing Ltd.

title: Safeguarding Public Health: Effective Management and Emerging Solutions for Foodborne Viral Diseases
authors: Sarkar I.
abstract: Foodborne viral diseases, caused by pathogens such as norovirus, hepatitis A, and rotavirus, pose significant public health challenges globally. These viruses are primarily transmitted through contaminated food, water, and surfaces, leading to widespread outbreaks and considerable health burdens. The epidemiology of these viruses reveals high incidences of illness, with norovirus being the leading cause of viral gastroenteritis and hepatitis A contributing to liver inflammation, particularly in regions with poor sanitation. Contamination at the source, including raw seafood and produce, coupled with inadequate food handling and hygiene practices, exacerbates the risk of viral transmission. Public health measures, including outbreak management and surveillance systems, are crucial in controlling these infections. International guidelines from organizations such as the WHO, FAO, and Codex Alimentarius, along with national regulations and standards, provide a framework for ensuring food safety. Food safety authorities like the FDA and EFSA play pivotal roles in enforcing these guidelines and responding to outbreaks. Emerging and re-emerging viruses, driven by globalization and environmental factors, present ongoing challenges. Advances in diagnostics, such as point-of-care tests and CRISPR-based detection, promise a more rapid and accurate identification of viral pathogens. Similarly, vaccination efforts, especially for hepatitis A, contribute significantly to disease prevention. Looking forward, the future of foodborne viral disease management includes enhancing diagnostic technologies, expanding vaccine coverage, and improving global surveillance and coordination. Addressing research gaps and implementing effective public health strategies will be essential in reducing the incidence of these diseases. By focusing on these areas, we can better manage foodborne viral infections, ultimately protecting public health and reducing the global burden of these pervasive pathogens. © 2026 selection and editorial matter, Priya Sutaoney, Priyambada Singh, Durgesh Nandini Chauhan, Nagendra Singh Chauhan, and Kamal Shah; individual chapters, the contributors.

title: Regional Disparities in Health, Physical, and Economic Parameters: A Decadal Analysis of North Bengal Districts
authors: Sengupta P.; Chakrabarti A.
abstract: This study tries to capture the trajectories of economic growth, inter-regional disparities, and socio-economic backwardness in terms of specific parameters in the districts of North Bengal over a decade. North Bengal has an advantageous location, which includes borders with Bangladesh, Nepal, and Bhutan, exhibiting considerable intra-regional disparities. The region has traditionally depended on tea, timber, and tourism, but is progressively shifting towards emerging sectors, including manufacturing, healthcare, and services. Public utilities such as clean drinking water and sanitation facilities are insufficient, especially in rural regions. Darjeeling, Jalpaiguri, and Cooch Behar perform comparatively better in terms of healthcare services, education, and basic needs parameters due to early investments and institutional development. However, the growth differential between southern districts and districts of the northern part of Bengal has remained pronounced. In contrast, North and South Dinajpur lag with basic amenities and human development metrics and continue to move upward on the development ladder. Malda remains industrially backwards, relying primarily on exports and agriculture, and having the best physical infrastructure compared to other districts of North Bengal. The primary concerns of the Northern region of West Bengal are the low literacy rate and a massive unskilled labour force. The overall composite index values of major socio-economic parameters and economic growth in all North Bengal districts reflect the backwardness of this region’s economy. These results showcase the need for region-specific inclusive policy interventions to address inequalities and promote balanced growth. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2025.

title: Groundwater Management and Governance in MENA Region
authors: Dawoud M.A.
abstract: The Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region is an arid and hyper arid region with nineteen countries/states with annual renewable freshwater per capita below water scarcity threshold (1000 m3/year). Groundwater is a key resource in the MENA region for improving water supply and agriculture uses. Due to the scarcity of renewable freshwater, increasing demand, and stress on surface water, nearly twelve states primarily depend on groundwater as a primary source of freshwater. Groundwater resources account for more than 80% of freshwater withdrawals in six states. There are 43 transboundary aquifer systems within the region. About 50% of the MENA region’s aquifer systems are non-renewable with over-abstraction which lead to sever drop in water table and deterioration in groundwater quality. In eight states, about 85% of agriculture irrigation water comes from groundwater compared to a global average of about 35% which also affects the food security. This is exacerbated by low water use productivity within the region with an average of about $0.25/m3 compared to $0.68/m3 globally. Groundwater valuation studies indicating that the economic value of groundwater is some states ranges between $0.52 and 0.85/m3. Economic valuation of groundwater supports planners and decision-makers in allocating and prioritizing available limited water resources in different developing sectors. Also, it will help in comparing between investing in groundwater protection with other environmental matters, and in balancing groundwater withdraw with conservation it for future generations. This chapter will assess how groundwater declining and deterioration due to increased demands, inefficient use and impacts of climate change should prompt MENA states to explore innovative and integrated governance frameworks to improve the management and ensure equitable access to strategic resources for both current and future generations. The groundwater importance for water security in the region should enhance the use of innovative technologies and dedicated funding towards integrated water resources management and heightened regional cooperation. Many countries in the region started to regulate groundwater resources with emphasis on allocation, well drilling, licensing, metering and sometimes pricing. However, the enforcement of these regulations is still weak. The depletion and quality deterioration of many aquifers are increasing the abstraction costs which affecting the social differentiation, as smaller farmers are pumped out and foreshadows a gradual collapse of the groundwater economy within the region. Few countries in the region still subside the groundwater abstraction which also affects the sustainability of this limited resource. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2025.

title: Blockchain-enabled Water Supply Chain Management: A Decentralized Approach to Sustainability and Efficiency
authors: Kousika N.; Ramani P.; Ramya V.; Akilandeeswari M.
abstract: This chapter explores how blockchain can transform water resource management, enabling an efficient decentralized solution to the global stream crisis. It highlights the role of blockchain in water distribution, sustainability and governance, along with the opportunities and challenges associated with its adoption. The integration of IoT and blockchain produces audit trails that make it easier to transparently gather and examine data that is decentralized and cannot be altered. The decentralized structure of blockchain makes it appropriate for locations without direct access to data centers. Water supply chain management is made more sustainable by ensuring equitable distribution, preventing waste and optimizing water logistics through the maintenance of an unchangeable record. IoT sensor and smart contract integration improves water distribution tracking in real time, automates regulatory compliance and guarantees fair water distribution. Additionally, the management of water rights is simplified, enabling equitable and legally verifiable transactions pertaining to the availability and use of water. © ISTE Ltd 2025. All rights reserved.

title: Sustainable Water Supply in Jaipur: Navigating Anthrospogenic Pressures for Geoheritage Conservation
authors: Poonia A.; Poonia M.
abstract: In the Anthropocene epoch, ensuring sustainable drinking water supply is paramount for both ecological resilience and human well-being. This study focuses on a heritage city of Jaipur, situated in the semi-arid western region of India, where groundwater plays a pivotal role in meeting water demands. Utilizing data from the Census of India 2011, Central Ground Water Board, and LANDSAT-ETM, the research highlights the critical importance of sustainable water management amid urbanization and shifting land use patterns. Analysis of observation wells data and Land Use Land Cover change identifies significant vulnerabilities in the central part of Jaipur district, particularly Jaipur city, underscoring challenges in maintaining sustainable water resources. The study further explores the urban–rural continuum through a comprehensive household survey, revealing disparities in drinking water access between urban and rural areas along this spectrum. The findings advocate for decentralized institutional frameworks and community-engaged monitoring to ensure equitable access, economic viability, and environmental sustainability in drinking water supply. By integrating local perspectives and data-driven approaches, this research contributes to understanding the human impacts on water resources in the context of geoheritage conservation and management. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2025.

title: The starvation in Gaza and implications on public health
authors: Ashour Y.; Iriqat D.; Parra-López C.; Hassoun A.
abstract: The famine in Gaza represents a case of deliberate and technologically enabled starvation resulting from sustained military actions that have destroyed food systems, obstructed aid, and targeted civilians seeking nourishment. Unlike natural disasters, this crisis demonstrates how digital and military technologies can be weaponized to enforce deprivation. Drawing on recent analyses of famine and mass starvation, including frameworks developed by the World Peace Foundation, this commentary conceptualizes Gaza’s famine as an instance of “engineered starvation,” in which artificial intelligence (AI), precision drones, and biometric surveillance are deployed to dismantle food, water, and energy systems. The resulting collapse has precipitated acute malnutrition, disease outbreaks, and long-term developmental harm, particularly among children and pregnant women. Beyond its immediate toll, this case signals a new paradigm in warfare—the algorithmic management of starvation—as a public health weapon. This analysis underscores the urgent need for global accountability mechanisms, protection of humanitarian infrastructure, regulation of military technologies in conflict zones, and the coordinated rebuilding of essential systems to prevent the normalization of famine as an instrument of war. © The Author(s) 2025.

title: Resilient communities: Navigating public health challenges in developing nations
authors: Saleh J.-E.A.
abstract: Resilient Communities: Navigating Public Health Challenges in Developing Nations explores how communities in resource-limited settings can overcome health inequities through resilience, innovation, and collective action. It examines key public health challenges, including communicable and non-communicable diseases, maternal and child health, healthcare access, and water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH). The book also highlights participatory approaches, disaster preparedness, gender equity, and the role of technology in transforming healthcare delivery. Through real-world case studies, it showcases successful community-driven initiatives and offers practical strategies for strengthening health systems, governance, and leadership. Key Features: - Analyzes public health challenges in developing nations. - Emphasizes community resilience and engagement. - Covers disease prevention, healthcare access, and digital health innovations. - Features case studies and evidence-based strategies. - Advocates for gender equity, sustainable development, and strong health governance. © 2025, Bentham Books imprint. All rights reserved.

title: Parallel Paths: Overseeing Two Pipeline Rehabilitation Projects in Southern California
authors: Toombs G.J.; Clemens K.
abstract: The Sepulveda Feeder pipeline is an integral part of the Metropolitan Water District of Southern California's (Metropolitan) Regional Water Distribution System. The 8-ft diameter pipeline extends approximately 42 mi from Granada Hills to the South Bay and supplies treated water to the City of Los Angeles, Santa Monica, Torrance, and the West Basin Municipal Water District's service areas. Metropolitan initially inspected the Sepulveda Feeder and assessed that the pipeline required rehabilitation at three locations. During the project, it was discovered that urgent rehabilitation was required on another pipeline in Metropolitan's distribution system in Orange County. Metropolitan determined that the sections of pipe required a standalone, fully structural internal rehabilitation. As a result, the utilization of Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer (CFRP) was found to be the most efficient in terms of cost, access, street-side disruption, and environmental impacts. This concurrent work was performed by a 20-person crew. Rehabilitation of this critical infrastructure will extend the service life of these pipe segments at least 50 years, per the American Water Works Association C305 Standard.  © ASCE.

title: Application of Nano-based Solutions for Water and Wastewater Management Through Science and Technological Innovations for Sustainable Environmental and Economic Growth
authors: Bhattacharya S.; Sachdev B.K.; Seth A.
abstract: Sustainable water and wastewater management might be a step closer with the help of nano-based technologies. Efficient monitoring and treatment options offered by nano-based systems offer a game-changing way to manage water and wastewater in a sustainable manner. To ensure that future generations have access to clean drinking water, it is essential to tackle current obstacles and encourage the ethical application of nanotechnology so that we may fully utilize its potential. Transparency, accuracy, and privacy protection must be ensured by legal frameworks that adapt to the usage of modern technologies. The use of nanosensors in the continuous monitoring of water quality is crucial. These sensors can identify pollutants at incredibly low concentrations because of their great sensitivity and selectivity. Examples of such membranes include carbon nanotube and graphene oxide membranes. Efficient removal of contaminants and recovery of resources are two examples of the improved treatment possibilities offered by nanomaterials. Nanomaterials provide unique legal issues in water treatment due to concerns over regulation, liability, and approval. In order to weigh the pros and cons of nano-based treatment approaches, laws should require thorough environmental impact evaluations. To guarantee the secure implementation of these technologies, further laws could be required. If there are any negative side effects from using nanosolutions to treat water and wastewater, the legal frameworks should spell out who is responsible. To deal with unanticipated outcomes, accountability mechanisms need to be set up. Ethical questions about the potential effects on human health, the environment, and society and the economy may arise in relation to water technologies based on nanotechnology. Responsible innovation and use can only be fostered if there are legal safeguards in place to deal with ethical concerns. Cooperation between nations is crucial in addressing water-related issues since they affect the entire world. In order to promote cooperation on nanosolutions, legal frameworks and agreements need to be in place to safeguard national rules while also promoting the exchange of information. Responsible and sustainable practices need addressing the legal problems that come with integrating nanotechnologies into water and wastewater management. Innovation can only flourish in an atmosphere where people’s health, the environment, and shared values are protected by dynamic regulatory frameworks. This review delves into the various ways nanotechnology is being used in water management, from monitoring to treatment. It also gives a quick rundown of the policy surrounding the use of nanosolutions for sustainable water and wastewater management, particularly in monitoring and treatment. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2025.

title: User Perception and Behaviour Towards the Sustainability of Shared Sanitation Facilities in Poorer Peri-Urban Area (Case Study: Ciwalengke, Majalaya District)
authors: Salimah H.; Nastiti A.; Roosmini D.
abstract: Access to safe sanitation is crucial for public health and sustainable development. The WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme recognizes the role of shared sanitation in achieving Sustainable Development Goal 6b. Shared sanitation facilities provide a practical solution in densely populated poorer areas and offer a cost-effective alternative to private facilities. However, their functional sustainability is often compromised by inadequate operation and maintenance. This study aims to identify psychosocial factors influencing the maintenance of shared sanitation facilities, focusing on a case study in Ciwalengke, Majalaya by employing the RANAS and IBM-WASH frameworks. The questionnaire components include behavioural, risk, attitude, norms, ability, self-regulation, contextual, psychosocial, and technology, which were reduced from several items within each variable using Principal Component Analysis (PCA). These components were used as predictor variables and analysed using multi-linear regression with the outcome variable as behaviour, resulting in an R2 value of 0.395 at p<0.01. Further analysis reveals that risks, attitude, and self-regulation components are significant predictors of behavioural outcomes. The sustainability analysis, based on questionnaire responses, indicates that sanitation facilities in the area are somewhat sustainable. These findings demonstrate that users' perceptions and behaviours provide valuable insights into assessing and enhancing the sustainability of shared sanitation facilities. © 2025 Institute of Physics Publishing. All rights reserved.

title: Mapping European innovation and policy landscapes using deep learning: Technologies for sustainable wastewater management
authors: Narang G.; Galdelli A.; Sospiro P.; Govindarajan U.H.; Mancini A.
abstract: Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), established by the United Nations in 2015, chart a global course toward sustainability, with Goal 6 specifically targeting the optimization of water resources to ensure widespread access to clean water and sanitation. The objective of this SDG mandates innovative approaches to managing wastewater, which is a critical component for the preservation of public health and our environment. Recent advancements across the technological landscape, including the Internet of Things (IoT), Computer Vision, and Artificial Intelligence (AI), have ushered in a new era for wastewater management, offering unprecedented capabilities in monitoring, data collection, and analysis at scale. These technologies have the potential to revolutionize traditional practices, enhance process efficiency, and play a crucial role in achieving SDG 6. This chapter explores the evolution of wastewater management strategies within the context of the regulation framework of the European Union. The methodology employs a comprehensive analysis and empirical review of 5550 patent grants collected from the years 2016-23 using KeyBERT and topic modeling to identify and categorize relevant patents. We then assess the alignment of these patents with the Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive of 2014 using cosine similarity metrics to evaluate the contextual relevance and technological alignment between them and select the most relevant patents. The analysis reveals an interest in digital innovations, as evidenced by the surge in patent grants in wastewater management. However, there is a gap between the potential of these theoretical advancements and their real-world implementation since only 68 patents show a high similarity rating with the policy document. Even in those cases, there is a weak similarity between the patents and the policy document, with most patents from outside European regions. This gap signifies not just a technological challenge but also highlights areas requiring European policy intervention, cross-sector collaboration, and knowledge sharing to bridge the divide between innovation and application. The proposed framework in the chapter will serve as a template for stakeholders in the industry to better align innovations to the needs proposed by experts in the government and to better draft streamlined policies. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved..

title: Exploring Climate Change Vulnerability of Nature-Based Destinations: A Systematic Review of Literature
authors: Kwinje C.; Mutizira P.; Baipai R.
abstract: Climate change poses severe impacts on Southern Africa’s nature-based destinations. Nature-based destinations are critical for biodiversity protection, cultural heritage preservation, and livelihoods in the local community. The purpose of this chapter is to explore the literature on the climate change vulnerability of nature-based destinations in Southern Africa. Using a qualitative methodology through desk research or document research, a sample of 46 journal papers from Scopus were reviewed. The results illustrate the complex effects of climate change on Southern African nature-based tourism, showing climate vulnerabilities in several areas in nature-based tourism destinations. Traditional seasons have become unstable due to changing weather patterns, which has decreased the attraction and accessibility of popular nature-based destinations in Southern Africa. This is especially the case during droughts and other harsh weather events that reduce the visibility of wildlife and tourism infrastructure. Because fewer people visit these destinations and livelihoods are disturbed, communities that depend on tourism lose money and experience increased poverty. Also, biodiversity is threatened, which impacts the iconic species and habitat integrity essential for wildlife tourism. Rising sea levels and coral bleaching further jeopardise coastal areas popular for nature activities like fishing, sea diving, and whitewater rafting. On the other hand, health risks from water scarcity and sanitation challenges pose additional deterrents to tourism. However, adaptive measures, such as sustainable water management, energy-efficient technologies, and eco-friendly practises in the tourism sector, are being implemented to mitigate these effects and enhance climate resilience. The findings highlight the need for a collaborative approach to climate change adaptation and sustainable development in nature-based destinations. It is recommended that government agencies enhance their institutional capacity, improve access to climate information, invest in climate-resilient infrastructure and engage and empower local communities. These actions may help respond more effectively to climate challenges and promote the sustainable development of nature-based destinations. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2025.

title: Agricultural Water Security: A Global Perspective
authors: Haj-Amor Z.
abstract: Agricultural Water Security: A Global Perspective offers a comprehensive exploration of the challenges and solutions surrounding sustainable water use in agriculture. Bridging the gaps between water availability, demand, and governance, this book examines the intricate connections between agricultural production, food security, and socioeconomic factors influencing water management decisions. Through global case studies and cutting-edge research, it presents strategies for balancing water supply and demand, improving water-use efficiency, and adapting to climate change and population growth. An indispensable resource for students, researchers, policymakers, and professionals in water and agricultural sciences, this book provides the insights needed to tackle the pressing issue of agricultural water security in an era of increasing water stress. Explores the physical, economic, and policy dimensions of agricultural water security, integrating global case studies and the latest research. Presents solutions for balancing water supply and demand, enhancing water-use efficiency, and adapting to climate change and population growth. Examines agricultural water security at farm, regional, national, and global levels, emphasizing integrated and sustainable management approaches. © 2026 Zied Haj-Amor. All rights reserved.

title: Enhancing waste management systems in Canada: Integration of geographic information system and remote sensing approaches
authors: Karimi N.; Richter A.; Wai Ng K.T.
abstract: Solid waste management in Canada faces growing challenges due to urbanization and population growth. Traditional methods are insufficient to handle the increasing waste volumes and associated environmental impacts. This chapter explores the integration of geographical information system (GIS) techniques and remote sensing (RS) indices to enhance waste management systems in Canada, focusing on optimizing landfill siting, monitoring environmental impacts, identifying fugitive gas hotspots, and improving accessibility to waste disposal services. Canadian case studies, mostly in prairie lands, demonstrate the application of these technologies for landfill site suitability and expansion, considering various environmental and human factors. The chapter also discusses using RS indices, like land surface temperature and vegetation indices, to monitor landfill impacts and identify environmental stressors. Additionally, the chapter presents methods for regionalizing waste management systems using GIS network analysis and satellite imagery, ensuring better coverage and accessibility, especially in remote areas. Challenges to adopting these technologies, including costs, complexity, and institutional barriers, are addressed, with strategies suggested for overcoming them. Finally, the critical role of GIS and RS in transforming waste management practices in Canada, offering a data-driven approach to improve sustainability and efficiency is highlighted. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, Anderson Assuah and Kelvin Tsun Wai Ng; individual chapters, the contributors.

title: Mapping Climate-Induced Risks in Maharashtra’s Rural Water Supply
authors: Mandal S.; Vaishnavi P.N.A.; Vharkat B.; Ghodke A.; Kabir Y.
abstract: The state of Maharashtra is prone to several climate hazards, including cyclones, landslides, droughts and floods. These natural hazards have serious implications for the performance of rural water supply systems through their adverse impacts on the quantity and quality of source water, the water supply infrastructure, and community's ability to access water supply sources. They affect the functioning of water supply schemes through the damage they cause to power supply systems. The composite index developed for assessing climate-induced water supply risk is used for assessing the risk in water supply induced by water-related climate hazards. The chapter first discusses the climate hazards in the state. It then systematically presents the data on various natural, physical, socioeconomic, and institutional and policy factors influencing climate risk in rural water supply for the state at the district level. It then presents the results of computation of climate risk at the district level and identify the districts that are highly prone to risks and then do a diagnosis to identify the factors that are actually contributing to the risks in those districts. © 2025 selection and editorial matter, M. Dinesh Kumar and Yusuf Kabir; individual chapters, the contributors.

title: Innovations and efficiency in wastewater treatment using artificial intelligence
authors: Ortiz J.A.; Zamudio-García V.M.
abstract: This document explores the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in optimizing wastewater treatment processes, focusing on key areas such as chemical dosing, aeration control, and sedimentation. The integration of advanced AI techniques, including neural networks, genetic algorithms, and optimization methods like Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and Bayesian Optimization, has significantly enhanced the efficiency and reliability of these processes. Through the implementation of machine learning models and real- time control systems, AI has enabled more precise adjustments, leading to reduced operational costs, improved resource management, and better compliance with environmental regulations. The study also highlights the potential for AI- driven innovations to further enhance sustainability in wastewater management, presenting opportunities for future research to expand on these advancements and address emerging challenges in the sector. © 2025, IGI Global Scientific Publishing. All rights reserved.

title: BOP entrepreneurship and environmental sustainability
authors: Bhogal N.; Hamann R.
abstract: In this chapter we explore the dual potential of base of the pyramid (BOP) entrepreneurship to impact the environment positively and negatively, emphasising the need for further research in this area. We highlight the intersection of BOP and environmental entrepreneurship, noting the challenges faced by entrepreneurs in BOP contexts, such as limited consumer purchasing power, infrastructure, and institutional voids, which can influence environmental practices. We review case studies demonstrating innovative responses to these challenges, in the energy, water and sanitation, agricultural, and waste management sectors. We identify key themes, including the role of tensions between economic and environmental objectives, the importance of social inclusion, and the embeddedness of entrepreneurs in local contexts. This chapter also calls for more research on the connections between BOP environmental entrepreneurship and informality, suggesting that brokers can play a crucial role in linking informal actors with formal markets while avoiding exploitative practices. © 2026 Miguel Rivera-Santos and Carlos Rufin.

title: GROUNDWATER RESOURCES AND SUSTAINABLE MANAGEMENT
authors: Zyder V.; Ameir O.; Mošová D.; Hubáček J.; Hrouda M.
abstract: Groundwater represents a vital yet often overlooked source of freshwater, essential for public water supply, agriculture, industry, and maintaining ecosystem functions. In the context of accelerating climate change, overexploitation, and water quality degradation, the sustainable management of groundwater resources is becoming increasingly important.
