title: Smart Vision Guided Table Sanitization System With Iot Integration for High-Traffic Dining Environments
authors: Tijare A.; Joshi A.; Shete D.; Kosurkar K.; Hariyani J.; Vyas H.
abstract: The procedures of table cleaning in high-traffic communal dining environments, such as temples, cafeterias, and institutional canteens, remain labour-intensive and inefficient, particularly during peak hours. While some automated or robotic cleaning systems have been explored, they often lack real-time contamination detection, and they are not tailored for the stringent hygiene requirements of such facilities. To address these limitations, this research presents an IoT-enabled table cleaning system that integrates real-time image processing with precise motor control for autonomous operation. The proposed architecture features a dual-controller setup, where the ESP32 microcontroller performs continuous image acquisition, contamination detection, manages BLE and Wi-Fi communication, and controls the cleaning mechanism and fluid dispensing mechanism. The system uses an ESP32-CAM module for capturing both pre- and post-cleaning images, enabling autonomous assessment of table cleanliness and re-cleaning if necessary. To detect objects and human presence, the ESP32-CAM is utilized. This ensures that cleaning only occurs when tables are unoccupied and free of obstructions. A fluid-level sensor in the spray reservoir and an under-table waste bin enhance both safety and operational reliability. Data on cleaning status and environmental conditions can be shared in real-time on cloud servers, supporting centralised monitoring and maintenance. Experimental evaluation demonstrates the system's high detection accuracy, cleaning efficiency with various debris types, and reliable communication across multiple tables. By enabling automated, verifiable, and remotely monitored table sanitation, the proposed system reduces manual labour, improves hygiene standards, and offers a scalable, sustainable solution for modern large-scale dining facilities. © 2025 IEEE.

title: Rebuilding trust and equity in Syria's health system: a governance-driven transition
authors: Alkhalil M.; Abbara A.; Dashash M.; Sullivan R.; Aboumayaleh M.; Ekzayez A.; Kharrat Z.; Obaydo R.H.; Alzoubi Z.; Alghatrif M.; Fouad F.M.

title: Prevention and Control Strategies for Swine Zoonoses
authors: Singh D.; Sharma P.; Gaur A.; Kant L.
abstract: Swine zoonoses, caused by pathogens such as bacteria, viruses, and parasites, pose significant public health and economic risks, particularly in regions with intensive pig farming. Key zoonotic diseases include brucellosis, leptospirosis, salmonellosis, and influenza. Despite advancements in pathogen control, the persistence of zoonotic pathogens and increasing antimicrobial resistance necessitate robust biosecurity, vaccination, and surveillance measures. Biosecurity practices, including controlled farm access, visitor management, and quarantine protocols, are critical for preventing disease transmission and reducing antibiotic use. Vaccination complements these measures by preserving herd health and minimizing zoonotic outbreaks. Surveillance systems enable early detection and effective management of diseases, supported by diagnostic tools, comprehensive health screenings, and accurate record-keeping. Additionally, vector control strategies targeting rodents, insects, and other carriers are essential to mitigate pathogen transmission. These integrated approaches align with the One Health framework, emphasizing the interconnectedness of animal, human, and environmental health, to ensure sustainable swine production and protect public health. Preventing disease in pig farms requires vector control, sanitation, biosecurity, and waste management. Key measures include integrated pest management, proper hygiene, manure handling, and regular cleaning. Biosecurity protocols and staff training ensure early disease detection and control. Effective waste management and compliance with environmental regulations minimize health risks and promote sustainability. © 2025 The Editor(s) (if applicable) and The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd.

title: Repurposing a traditional water resources management tool for the sanitation sector
authors: Abiodun O.A.; Ayeleru O.O.
abstract: The sanitation sector faces challenges, including inadequate infrastructure, resource constraints, and fragmented governance. This article explores the potential of repurposing Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) tools, traditionally used in the water sector, to address these issues. By leveraging IWRM principles—such as integrated planning, stakeholder participation, and adaptive management—this study proposes a framework to improve sanitation systems' efficiency, sustainability, and resilience. The article reviews recent literature (2016-24), identifies gaps, and presents case studies, including Singapore's NEWater Program and Nairobi's fecal sludge-to-energy initiatives, to demonstrate the applicability of IWRM tools in sanitation. Findings suggest that repurposing IWRM tools can enhance wastewater management, resource recovery, and equitable service delivery, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This study contributes by providing a comprehensive framework for integrating IWRM tools into sanitation systems, offering practical insights for policymakers and practitioners. The article concludes with recommendations for future research and practice, emphasizing the potential of smart sanitation systems and the circular economy to advance sustainable sanitation. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. title: Risk management and safety auditing in anaerobic digestion: Driving operational excellence
authors: Nagi G.E.; Hassanein A.
abstract: Anaerobic digestion (AD) has emerged as a game-changing technology, revolutionizing renewable energy generation and sustainable waste management by unlocking the energy potential of organic waste streams. By converting organic matter such as agricultural residues, industrial process by-products, and municipal biosolids into biogas and nutrient-rich digestate, AD provides significant environmental and economic benefits. However, the safe and efficient operation of AD facilities requires rigorous auditing procedures and robust safety standards tailored to specific contexts. These operations require a cohesive approach, integrating thorough auditing practices, comprehensive safety protocols, and advanced technological tools to streamline processes, minimize risks, and enhance overall reliability. Challenges vary across agricultural, industrial, and municipal AD systems. Agricultural systems often face seasonal feedstock variability and nutrient management demands, industrial systems must manage uniform but large-volume waste streams under stringent workplace regulations, and municipal systems require integration with sludge stabilization and odor control protocols. These diverse needs demand tailored audits to address feedstock characteristics, regulatory compliance, and operational scalability. Effective compliance and risk management frameworks rooted in ISO standards, Hazard and Operability (HAZOP) studies, and structured emergency action plans enable facilities to safeguard worker safety, maintain environmental integrity, and ensure process stability. AD facilities face numerous safety challenges, including the risks of drowning and falls near open tanks, as well as biogas-related hazards such as asphyxiation and fire. Addressing these dangers requires confined space entry protocols, robust electrical system safeguards, and comprehensive safety measures that tackle chemical, mechanical, and thermal risks. Employing protective equipment, enforcing lockout/tagout procedures, and utilizing real-time hazard monitoring systems are essential practices that enhance safety and mitigate risks effectively. Predictive maintenance, artificial intelligence (AI), and immersive training platforms play pivotal roles in reinforcing proactive safety cultures within AD operations. These technologies interact by providing real-time data insights, automating adjustments to process variables, and enhancing workforce preparedness through realistic simulations, creating a cohesive framework for safety and efficiency. These technologies, combined with best practices and case studies, reveal tangible benefits, including improved biogas yields, reduced downtime, and stronger community relations. Through the integration of rigorous auditing processes and advanced technologies, AD operators can unlock the full potential of the process, driving innovation, enhancing sustainability, and paving the way for a resilient and cleaner future. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved..

title: Bridging the Health Divide: A Policy Perspective on Indigenous Healthcare in Bangladesh
authors: Mamun A.A.
abstract: Background: Indigenous populations in Bangladesh—often referred to as Adibashi or Upojati—experience persistent health disparities. Geographic isolation, linguistic and cultural exclusion, and poverty drive these disparities. These communities, estimated at over two million, report considerably higher rates of maternal mortality, undernutrition, and limited access to institutional healthcare. This situation persists despite constitutional protections and national development goals. Objective: This perspective examines the structural, cultural, and policy-level barriers to healthcare access among Bangladesh's tribal communities. It also proposes evidence-based, inclusive strategies designed to achieve health equity. Methods: A narrative review approach was guided by the SANRA checklist. Literature was identified through PubMed, Google Scholar, and government portals. Sources included national surveys, ethnographic studies, and comparative policy models from Canada, Nepal, and the Philippines. Key themes analyzed were infrastructure deficits, workforce shortages, traditional medicine, linguistic barriers, and WASH access. A SWOT framework synthesizes insights and informs recommendations. Key Findings: Tribal health inequities in Bangladesh stem from weak infrastructure, cultural exclusion, workforce shortages, and poor health governance. International models show the benefits of decentralized, culturally adapted, community-led care. Conclusion: Achieving SDG 3 for indigenous populations requires urgent political commitment, targeted investment, and inclusive planning. Priorities include the establishment of a Tribal Health Desk, integration of traditional medicine, mobile health delivery, and culturally adapted training. Advancing indigenous health equity aligns with constitutional commitments and global standards of public health justice. © 2025 The Author(s). Health Science Reports published by Wiley Periodicals LLC.

title: Water and wastewater applications in developed and developing countries: extant experience and plan for the future
authors: Ogunro O.B.; Fakayode A.E.; Joseph O.J.
abstract: Water and wastewater management are crucial for sustaining growing populations while ensuring environmental sustainability. Developed nations benefit from advanced infrastructure, robust regulatory frameworks, and cutting-edge technologies such as membrane filtration, desalination, and wastewater reuse. These measures enhance water efficiency and sustainability, particularly in water-scarce regions. In contrast, developing countries struggle with inadequate infrastructure, financial limitations, and rapid urbanization, resulting in water pollution and limited clean water access. However, emerging solutions such as decentralized treatment systems, rainwater harvesting, and affordable filtration technologies offer promising alternatives, though they require more substantial policy support and investment to scale effectively. In modern water management, technological advancements function critically. The artificial intelligence, internet of things, and big data analytics optimize water distribution and treatment in developed nations, thereby improving efficiency and reducing losses. Meanwhile, resource-limited regions increasingly adopt cost-effective technologies like solar desalination and small-scale filtration systems to enhance water security. Governance and policy frameworks significantly impact water management, with strong institutions and enforcement ensuring sustainability in developed nations. In contrast, weak governance, corruption, and political instability often hinder progress in developing countries. Climate change further complicates water security, exacerbating worldwide droughts, floods, and water stress. Adaptive strategies such as circular economy models, integrated water resource management, and sustainable financing mechanisms are essential for long-term resilience. This chapter highlights the significance of innovation, policy reform, and international cooperation in bridging the gap between developing and developed nations. Nations can move toward a future of equitable and sustainable water management by implementing scalable solutions and strengthening governance structures. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved..

title: Complexities of the urban drinking water systems in Ethiopia and possible interventions for sustainability
authors: Beker B.A.; Kansal M.L.
abstract: Rapid urbanization in developing countries has imposed threats and challenges to basic urban infrastructures like drinking water, transportation, and energy systems. The existing urban drinking water systems (UDWS) are highly stressed and unsustainable, particularly under changing hydroclimatic conditions, population growth, changing socioeconomic conditions, government decisions, and various policies. This study focuses on the complexities of UDWS in Sub-Saharan African countries, especially in Ethiopia. The objective of this study is to investigate the issues and challenges of urban drinking water systems (UDWS) in Ethiopia, specifically, to assess the gap between water supply and demand, water loss/non-revenue water, environmental, technical, institutional, and governance, etc. and propose sustainable interventions to deal with such issues so as to improve. For this purpose, a mix of methods involving primary data (including key informant interviews, field observations, and field measured data) and secondary data (including published articles, books, various reports, and design documents), as well as various computer-aided applications (mainly, ArcGIS and WaterGEMS) are used to collect data. The issues are deliberated through the UDWSs of Addis Ababa, Adama, Mekelle, and Dire Dawa cities in Ethiopia. Complexities like water shortage, high and low pressure in the water distribution network (WDN), non-revenue water (NRW)/water loss, source pollution, ineffective policies and governance, and weak institutions are the main challenges to Ethiopian cities' water utilities. Further, the case study noticed that in Addis Ababa alone, potable water is only accessible to 66% of the city population. A significant water supply deficit was observed in Mekelle city, where only half of the city population has access to potable water from the system. Additionally, in Addis Ababa, Adama, Mekelle, and Dire Dawa, above 35% of the freshwater produced is either NRW, unaccounted for, or lost, which is significantly higher than the upper 25% limit suggested by the World Bank. Therefore, it is recommended to adopt certain sustainable interventions, such as integrated water resource management, installing appurtenances like pressure-reducing valves, check valves in the WDN, controlling and monitoring of WDN through supervisory control and data acquisition and Internet of Things, effective and long-term planning and policy, etc. It is felt that the study will help the decision-makers and the operators of the UDWS utilities to run the water supply schemes in a sustainable manner. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature B.V. 2023.

title: Determinants of diarrhea prevalence among children under 5 years in semi-arid Ghana
authors: Pienaah C.K.A.; Yoshida Y.; Saaka S.A.; Ategeeng F.N.; Luginaah I.
abstract: Despite the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG6) of achieving universal access to clean water and sanitation by 2030, many developing countries still face water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH)-related health issues such as child mortality caused by diarrhea. This study inves-tigated the factors contributing to diarrhea prevalence in rural children, utilizing a cross-sectional survey (n ¼ 517) of smallholder household representatives from a Risk, Attitudes, Norms, Abilities, and Self-Regulation (RANAS) perspective. Using binary logistic regression, the study found that a high prevalence of diarrhea among children was associated with unsafe/open disposal of child feces, living in the poorest house-holds, poor self-rated health, and residing in the Wa East district. Conversely, children from the Brifo ethnicity and those from larger households were less likely to have a high prevalence of diarrhea. These findings underscore the influence of behavioral, socio-cultural, and socioeconomic factors on the prevalence of diarrhea in rural areas. To achieve SDG6, child-friendly sanitation infrastructure, behavior change communication strategies, and incentivizing WASH infrastructure in Ghana and other regions in Sub-Saharan Africa facing similar conditions are recommended. © 2024 The Authors.

title: A Conceptual Framework for Managing Public Services Delivered by Environmental Enterprises in Informal Settlements
authors: Adewunmi Y.; Simbanegavi P.; Weaich M.
abstract: Informal settlements are frequently located in hazardous areas with a high risk of natural disasters. Upgrading informal settlements can be difficult due to the time and expense needed to complete the process. This chapter advocates using a management framework of public services in informal settlements. In doing so, it addresses 17 of the 17 UN sustainable development goals (SDGs). The study reviewed the literature to investigate current ways of managing environmental enterprises in informal settlements in South Africa. Thereafter, the challenges of managing public services were explored, and a conceptual framework for managing public services by social enterprises in such communities was developed. The chapter found that environmental enterprises are classified as ‘green spaces’ and infrastructure, water and sanitation services, energy systems, and recycling initiatives. Essential aspects of sustainable community-based facilities management (SCbFM) for managing public services are maintenance, governance, community project management, environment service delivery, service performance, governance, community project management, environment service delivery, service performance, well-being and health and safety, disaster management, and finance. Some of the problems of managing public services in informal settlements include the limited skills of managers, the focus of government on new projects rather than managing existing projects, not choosing the right indicators to measure service performance, and limited guidelines for the health and safety of managers and disaster management. Thus, a new conceptual framework was needed and developed based on the principles of social capital and capability for managing services in informal settlements in South Africa. © 2024 A. Vinodan, S. Mahalakshmi, and S. Rameshkumar.

title: Ion-selective supramolecular membrane with pH-regulated smart nanochannels for lithium extraction
authors: Gan N.; Lin Y.; Zhang Y.; Qiu Y.; Yu J.; She Q.; Ooya T.; Lin Q.; Matsuyama H.
abstract: Tunable gating ion-conducting membranes with high water permeability and precise ion selectivity remain urgently demanded in smart nanofiltration for efficient lithium extraction. Herein, inspired by the filtration function of protein channels, we report a smart and high-performance supramolecular membrane constructed via coordination between quaternary ammonium ligands (m-phenylenediamine/polyethyleneimine) and metal ion center (Cu2+). The pore architecture of the supramolecular membrane is dynamic and can be switched by applying pH stimulus, where coordinated interchain expands when exposed to acidic operating conditions and induces concomitantly reinforced electrostatic exclusion due to enhanced local charge density. The tunable gating regularity enables operando modulation of precise ionic separation in situ. The resulting membrane exhibits significantly enhanced water permeance (19.8 L m−2 h−1·bar−1) and simultaneously promoted Li+/Mg2+ selectivity (RMg2+ = 96.4 %), surpassing typical trade-off between permeability and selectivity at pH 3 condition. This study demonstrates the amazing capability of environmental-responsive regulation of membrane pore-channel structure, and provides inspiration for engineering advanced supramolecular membranes for lithium extraction and beyond. © 2024 Elsevier B.V.

title: There and back again: dynamics of temporary labor migration, insights from rural India
authors: Attah-Otu B.; Sengupta A.; McAleavy T.
abstract: Temporary labor migration is a household phenomenon among rural communities in India. This study seeks to understand the subjective experiences influencing the temporariness of labor migration among internal migrants in India by examining various factors such as migration conditions, motivation, migration arrangements, coping and adaptation strategies, and determinants of stay. To achieve this objective, the current qualitative study utilized 14 in-depth interviews and 2 focus group discussions to investigate the temporary nature of labor migration among internal migrants in India. Our findings reveal that migration decisions are rational choices made collectively at the household level, considering socio-economic outcomes. We also find that social networks and contractors facilitate migration arrangements and job connections, and migrants employ various strategies to reduce costs and cope with expenses in urban areas. However, migration destinations often fail to meet migrants’ expectations, exposing them to low-wage employment and precarious working and living conditions, which are detrimental to their health. Limited housing and sanitation facilities further contribute to the challenges faced by migrants. Work conditions, including poor wages and high job demands, also affect their well-being. These findings highlight the need for improved support systems that address accommodation challenges, work conditions, and the overall welfare of labor migrants.
